extracted.intended_audience: members of the public and stakeholders (educators, school districts, organizations) who want to view or submit public comments on TEA proposed rules
extracted.subtask_short: submit public comment on TEA rules
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for members of the public on when, how, and where to submit comments on proposed Texas Education Agency rules (commissioner, SBOE, SBEC), what happens to submitted comments, and exceptions for emergency rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a public comment
rubrics_metrics.description: A public comment is an opportunity for any interested person to submit data, views, or arguments on a proposed rule. The opportunity for public comment is required by state law, Texas Government Code, §2001.029.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing — when the public comment period begins
rubrics_metrics.description: The public comment period on a rule begins when the rule is published as proposed in the Texas Register.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the triggering event for comment periods across commissioner, SBOE, and SBEC proposed rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comment period length — commissioner of education rules
rubrics_metrics.description: For commissioner of education rules, the comment period lasts 31 days unless another date is specified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submit comments within the 31-day window unless the proposed rule explicitly sets a different deadline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comment period length and testimony opportunity — State Board of Education (SBOE) rules
rubrics_metrics.description: For State Board of Education (SBOE) rules, the comment period is at least 31 days and lasts through the next regular SBOE meeting where the SBOE will take second reading action and the public can also provide testimony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The public may both submit written comments during the period and give oral testimony at the specified SBOE meeting that falls within the comment window.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comment period length and meeting opportunity — State Board for Educator Certification (SBEC) rules
rubrics_metrics.description: For State Board for Educator Certification (SBEC) rules, the comment period lasts 31 days, but the public also has an opportunity to provide input at the next regular SBEC meeting where the SBEC will take action to adopt the proposed rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Written comments must be submitted during the 31-day comment period; additionally, stakeholders may present input at the SBEC meeting where adoption is considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to submit a public comment (methods)
rubrics_metrics.description: Forms for submitting public comments are available on the TEA website (proposed commissioner rules page, proposed SBOE rules page, and proposed SBEC rules page). Comments on a proposal may also be submitted to Rulemaking Unit, Texas Education Agency, 1701 North Congress Avenue, Austin, Texas 78701.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the specific web form for the rule type (commissioner/SBOE/SBEC) when available; postal submissions may be sent to the Rulemaking Unit address provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Where to view proposed rules
rubrics_metrics.description: All proposed rules of the commissioner, SBOE, and SBEC are posted on the TEA website after filed as proposed with the Texas Register. Proposed rules are available on the proposed commissioner rules web page, proposed SBOE rules web page, and proposed SBEC rules web page.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check the appropriate proposed-rules page on the TEA site to read the exact text of a proposed rule before deciding to comment.

rubrics_metrics.name: What happens to submitted public comments (compilation and forwarding)
rubrics_metrics.description: The TEA compiles the public comments received during a proposed rule's public comment period and provides those summaries of and responses to the public comments to the appropriate rulemaking body--commissioner, SBOE, or SBEC--for consideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TEA acts as the collector and summarizer of comments and forwards summaries and any TEA responses to the decision-making body for their consideration in rule adoption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content and attribution requirements for comment summaries (Texas Government Code §2001.033)
rubrics_metrics.description: Texas Government Code, §2001.033, requires the summary of a comment to include the name of the group or association that commented and whether it was for or against the adoption of the rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When TEA summarizes comments, group/association submissions will be identified by name along with their position; individuals will be included in summaries but will not be named.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of individual comments in summaries
rubrics_metrics.description: Comments from individuals will also be included in the summary of public comments, but individuals will not be named.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Individual submissions are represented in aggregate or by content without personal identification in the official summary provided to the rulemaking body.

rubrics_metrics.name: Required responses when the rulemaking body disagrees with comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Texas Government Code, §2001.033, requires that if the rulemaking body disagrees with the comment, the response to the comment must include the reasons why the rulemaking body disagreed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Official responses must explain the rationale for rejecting or disagreeing with substantive public comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possible effect of comments when the rulemaking body agrees
rubrics_metrics.description: If the rulemaking body agrees with the comment, it could result in a change to the proposed rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submitted comments may lead to revisions in the text of the rule prior to adoption; summaries and responses reflecting changes are included with the adopted rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication of summaries and responses with the adopted rule
rubrics_metrics.description: The summaries of and responses to public comments are included with the adopted rule published in the Texas Register.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After adoption, interested persons can review the published summaries and the rulemaking body's responses in the Texas Register alongside the final adopted rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emergency rule exception (no public comment period)
rubrics_metrics.description: An emergency rule is not required to have a public comment period and may be effective as soon as it is filed with the Texas Register. Texas Government Code, §2001.034, allows a state agency to adopt an emergency rule if it finds that an imminent peril to the public health, safety, or welfare, or a requirement of state or federal law, requires adoption of a rule on fewer than 30 days' notice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emergency rules bypass the normal comment period when an agency makes the statutory finding; agencies may use emergency rules when immediate action is legally required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duration limit for emergency rules
rubrics_metrics.description: An emergency rule may be effective up to 180 days.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emergency rules are temporary measures limited in duration to a maximum of 180 days unless further action is taken under normal rulemaking procedures.
